fly.h2: Learn to fly the Chupito before your first real throw

image.alt: The TBS Chupito in Nanawing, seen from the chase camera as it banks low over the Island, with the OSD showing speed and battery
image.caption: The Chupito in Nanawing, chase view. Switch to FPV when you’re ready. Reference airframe by {maker}.

items: Snap it round: flick it from bank to bank with small stick inputs. It rolls at 360°/s, the quickest roll in the hangar.
Keep your speed up: open it up to 140 km/h on the straights. It stalls at 35 km/h, so carry speed through the turns and ease it down to land.
Race it: Windmill Run and River Run on the Island, Tunnel Run and Pyramid Run in the Desert, then Estate Run through Parkland’s giant oaks, 2.8 km. Set a lap time, then beat it.

blocks.h3: Fly it with what you have
items: Keyboard, gamepad or your own USB RC radio on a laptop; two thumb sticks on your phone. No gaming PC needed.
No radio? Fly it clean on the keyboard: tap for a nudge, hold for full stick. Space throws it over your head, and the iNAV-style OSD keeps your battery in view.
It stalls at 35 km/h. A slow, tight turn is how a Chupito stalls: keep the speed up and start the turn early.
The roll is quick. Small inputs, then wait.
Landing: ease it down with a little throttle in. Chop it early and it drops. After a crash, reset and go again, then take it to the field.

variants.name: Chupito Kit
variants.sub: Build it with the parts you choose
variants.includes: The EPP wing, carbon spars, glass-fibre motor and camera mounts, metal hardware and the sticker sheet. You bring every part that moves or lights up.
variants.pick: Pick it if you already have a motor, an AIO board or ESC, servos, GPS and a receiver, or want to choose every part yourself. TBS also sells the electronics package on its own.
variants.none: TBS ships the bare kit from its own store. At the last check, no Indian seller we check lists it.

image.alt: The TBS Chupito Kit’s airframe parts laid out: the fuselage pod, both wing panels, the fin, the hatch and the spars

variants.name: Chupito PNP
variants.sub: Fly on electronics matched to the wing
variants.includes: Everything in the Kit plus TBS’s electronics: the AIO flight-controller and ESC board, GPS, motor, servos and prop. You add your video system (DJI O3 or O4, Walksnail or analogue), a receiver such as a Crossfire Nano RX, and a 4S–6S pack of 800–1800 mAh under 270 g. Team BlackSheep’s own store calls it the Set.
variants.pick: Pick it for your first Chupito: the electronics are matched to the wing, and TBS publishes iNAV settings for them.
variants.none: At the last check, no Indian seller we check lists the PNP on its own.

image.alt: The TBS Chupito with its electronics package: two servos, the flight-controller and ESC board, the motor, the GPS and the propeller

variants.name: Chupito Crash-A-Lot
variants.sub: Keep flying after a hard landing
variants.includes: The PNP’s airframe and electronics, plus spare foam parts to swap in after a hard landing.
variants.pick: Pick it if this is your first wing, or your field is unforgiving.
variants.none: At the last check, no Indian seller we check lists the Crash-A-Lot.

groups.h3: Keep the camera and VTX where you put them

items.title: TBS Chupito 800 Pan-Tower
items.what: Pan the camera on a Feetech FT90M servo and look into the turn. It is the mount Team BlackSheep links from the kit page, and the designer links a DJI O4 Pro mount for it.
items.alt: TBS Chupito 800 Pan-Tower, the 3D print by ninjamic85 on MakerWorld

items.title: TBS Chupito camera pod with a lock
items.what: A camera pod that locks between the battery-tray ribs, so a hard throw can’t push the VTX assembly back. Lift the lock with a finger to take it out.
items.alt: TBS Chupito camera pod with a lock, the 3D print by DJISilesia on Thingiverse

items.title: TBS Chupito VTX Cage lock
items.what: A 2 g TPU block that stops the stock VTX support sliding back when you throw.
items.alt: TBS Chupito VTX Cage lock, the 3D print by JP75 on MakerWorld

items.title: TBS Chupito O4 Pro 10 degree soft mount
items.what: Soft-mounts a DJI O4 Pro on M2 gummies, tilts it 10° down and leaves room for ND filters.
items.alt: TBS Chupito O4 Pro 10 degree soft mount, the 3D print by BobbyFPV on MakerWorld

groups.h3: A hatch and a battery that stay put

items.title: TBS Chupito Battery Holder
items.what: Lets shorter 5-inch quad packs sit tight under the stock strap. One version takes an Ummagrip plate, so the CG stays where you set it from pack to pack.
items.alt: TBS Chupito Battery Holder, the 3D print by FPV Tribe on MakerWorld

items.title: TBS Chupito Battery Tray 2 Stap
items.what: A TPU tray with two straps in the middle, for when the single stock strap won’t hold a balanced pack.
items.alt: TBS Chupito Battery Tray 2 Stap, the 3D print by GibroniFPV on Thingiverse

items.title: Screw Down Hatch for Team BlackSheep Chupito
items.what: If the foam hatch is gone, this one screws down with an M3 instead of clipping. Stretch it 2mm before printing; the designer’s page says why.
items.alt: Screw Down Hatch for Team BlackSheep Chupito, the 3D print by GibroniFPV on Thingiverse

groups.h3: Protect the fins, servos and wings

items.title: TBS Chupito Bottom Fin Slider

items.alt: TBS Chupito Bottom Fin Slider, the 3D print by FPV Tribe on MakerWorld

items.title: Servo air cover TBS Chupito

logs.h2: Analyse your Chupito flight logs in 3D

image.alt: The log viewer replaying its sample flight over red and tan canyon country on a 3D globe, with a TBS Chupito in the 3D view and the AI flight analysis beside it
image.caption: The log viewer’s built-in sample flight on a 3D globe, with the AI flight analysis beside it.

paragraphs: Drop your Chupito’s log into the log viewer and fly the flight again on a 3D globe, with the charts alongside. See where the nose dropped before that wobble, and what the battery did on the long climb.

Then let the AI flight analysis write it up: what happened, the evidence, and what to check before your next flight, in plain English you can share. It’s in beta and reads only an anonymous summary of the flight’s numbers; your log file never leaves your machine.
Most Chupitos fly iNAV, and the log viewer reads its blackbox logs. Betaflight blackbox logs and the telemetry CSV from your EdgeTX radio’s SD card work too. Free, in your browser.

links.label: Turn on logging in EdgeTX, Betaflight or iNAV

logs.note: Reads iNAV blackbox logs from 9.x and earlier, and Betaflight up to 4.5.

items.q: Is this the real TBS Chupito?
items.a: It’s Nanawing’s recreation of Team BlackSheep’s 800mm wing, with the same span and shape. It is not an official TBS simulator. Practise the habits here; the kit itself comes from Team BlackSheep.

items.q: Do I need an RC radio?
items.a: No. Fly on the keyboard, a gamepad or your own USB RC radio. On the keyboard, tap for a nudge and hold for full stick.

items.q: Does it work on a phone?
items.a: Yes. Open the same link on your phone and fly with two thumb sticks on the screen.

items.q: Is it free, and do I have to install anything?
items.a: It’s free and runs in your browser: no install, no login. After the first visit it works offline too.

items.q: Where can I buy a TBS Chupito in India?
items.a: Compare Chupito prices and stock at Indian hobby sellers on Wings, then buy from each seller’s page.

link.label: Compare TBS Chupito prices in India

items.q: What’s the difference between the Chupito Kit, PNP and Crash-A-Lot?
items.a: The Kit is the airframe on its own: you add every electronic part. The PNP adds TBS’s electronics package, matched to the wing (Team BlackSheep’s store calls it the Set). The Crash-A-Lot is the PNP plus a spare set of foam parts.

items.q: Where is the TBS Chupito manual, and how do I set it up in iNAV?
items.a: Team BlackSheep publishes the Chupito manual and its suggested iNAV settings for the Chupito’s electronics. Mads Tech’s video above walks through the build and the iNAV setup.

items.q: Are there 3D-printed parts for the Chupito?
items.a: Yes. Pilots have shared prints for the camera, battery, hatch and fins on MakerWorld and Thingiverse.

items.q: How do I analyse my Chupito flight logs?
items.a: Drop your iNAV or Betaflight blackbox log, or your EdgeTX radio’s telemetry CSV, into the log viewer. Fly the flight again on a 3D globe with the charts alongside, and let the AI flight analysis, in beta, tell you what happened in plain English. Free in your browser. Your log file never leaves your machine; the AI analysis gets only an anonymous summary of the numbers.

faqNote: Sim time is no substitute for instruction, aircraft checks or safe flying at the field.
